description: I created my app while volunteering at a local Austin event.
summary:
Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA Earth science visualizations into interactive music. I built a web app that scans each image from west to east and translates its color, position, brightness, texture, and visual intensity into pitch, rhythm, instruments, volume, and stereo placement. It includes 23 NASA-based “records,” live visual feedback, shuffle and queue modes, downloadable audio, and a Studio Mixer where listeners can change the scale, tempo, tone, reverb, and instruments—from orchestral strings and guitars to Star Trek-inspired scanner pings. Users can also upload their own images and hear them interpreted using the same rules.

This addresses the challenge by making Earth information something people can not only see, but hear, explore, and remix. It creates another way into complex NASA data—especially for students, curious non-scientists, and people who benefit from alternatives to purely visual communication. The goal is to make learning about our planet approachable, memorable, and fun.
details:
Earth Information Jukebox is a browser-based experience that turns NASA Earth science imagery into music. Instead of adding a prerecorded soundtrack, the app analyzes each image and generates the sound from the picture itself. It reduces the image to a grid and scans from west to east. Horizontal position controls time and stereo placement, vertical position controls pitch, and properties such as color, brightness, texture, and visual intensity affect the instruments, volume, note length, and tone.

The app currently includes 33 NASA-based records organized into two collections: Earth Right Now and Earth Portraits. As each record plays, a moving playhead and animated markers show which parts of the image are producing sound. Listeners can repeat a record, play the collection in order, or use a visible shuffle queue. They can also download a generated loop or upload their own image.

The Studio Mixer makes the experience more playful. Users can change the musical key, scale, tempo, note density, tone, reverb, and instruments. Instrument choices include orchestral ensembles, individual strings, acoustic and electric guitars, and bright science-fiction-inspired scanner tones.

I built the project with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using the Web Audio API for real-time sound synthesis/ Canvas for the visualization. It runs entirely in the browser without specialized hardware. I packaged it as a container using Docker and Nginx, published the image through Docker Hub, and deployed it on my OpenShift cluster. The interface uses a Carbon inspired design with responsive light and dark themes.

The main benefit is that people can experience Earth information in another way. It can help students and curious non-scientists explore patterns that might otherwise feel technical or distant, while also supporting people who benefit from alternatives to purely visual communication.

I considered accessibility, mobile browser behavior, performance, NASA attribution, and scientific integrity. The app clearly describes the sonification rules and treats the result as an accessible artistic interpretation—not as a scientific measurement instrument. My intended impact is to make learning about Earth feel approachable, memorable, and genuinely fun.
